title: Protein structure and function; Amino acids and peptide bonds
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM07#t4 term and clue written for the game; BM07#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM08a#t3 term and clue written for the game; BM08a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM07#N.2a, BM08a#N.4a, BM07#N.4a, BM08a#N.10a, BM07#N.6a, BM08a#N.13, BM07#N.13.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Polypeptide
items.clue: Many protein monomers joined in one chain

items.label: Amino acids
items.clue: The monomers of proteins, each built around a central carbon atom

items.label: Tertiary structure
items.clue: Overall 3D shape of one folded chain, held by bonds between R groups

items.label: α-helix
items.clue: Coil of the chain in which backbone hydrogen bonds hold each turn to the next

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by all 20 of the amino acids that are coded for in the genetic code?

options.text: The R-group is identical in every amino acid, and the amine and carboxyl groups are what vary.
An amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R-group are all bonded to one alpha carbon atom.
The amine group is bonded directly to the carbon atom of the carboxyl group, with no carbon between.
The amine group is an NH₃ group, with the same structure as a molecule of ammonia.

questions.explanation: This is the general structure: a central (alpha) carbon carrying the amine group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R-group. Only the R-group differs between the 20.

questions.stem: What stabilises the alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets of a protein's secondary structure?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds at regular positions between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone.
Ionic bonds between charged amine and carboxyl groups spaced regularly along the backbone.
Disulfide bonds between cysteines spaced at regular intervals along the polypeptide.
Hydrogen bonds forming the peptide links between the amine and carboxyl groups of neighbours.

questions.explanation: Helices and sheets are held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one peptide bond and the N–H of another, at regular positions along the backbone.

questions.stem: Two amino acids react to form a dipeptide. Which statement describes this reaction?

options.text: The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amine group of the other, and water is released.
A molecule of water is taken in to provide the atoms needed to link the two amino acids together.
The R-group of one amino acid bonds to the R-group of the other, forming the peptide bond between them.
The amine group of one amino acid forms a hydrogen bond with the carboxyl group of the other, and no water is released.

questions.explanation: Condensation: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water. The peptide bond forms between the carbon of the carboxyl group and the nitrogen of the amine group.

questions.stem: When egg white is heated, its soluble proteins turn into a white solid. What has happened to the protein molecules?

options.text: Heat has broken the bonds holding their folded shape, so they have unfolded.
Heat has broken the peptide bonds, so the polypeptides have been split into amino acids.
Heat has killed the proteins, so they are no longer able to carry out their functions.
Heat has changed their shape temporarily, and they will refold as soon as the egg white cools.

questions.explanation: This is denaturation. Extra vibration breaks the bonds that hold the 3D shape; the unfolded chains tangle together, so the egg white becomes an insoluble solid.

questions.stem: A polypeptide of 150 amino acids is assembled by condensation reactions. How does the number of water molecules change as the whole chain is formed?

options.text: 150 released
298 released
149 released
149 consumed

questions.explanation: Each condensation forms one peptide bond and releases one water molecule. A chain of 150 needs 149 bonds: 149 water molecules.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces one amino acid in an enzyme at a position on the surface far from the active site in the folded protein. The enzyme loses most of its activity. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The result must be an error, because only the amino acids of the active site itself can affect catalysis
The change disturbs interactions that hold the enzyme's overall shape, altering the active site
The loss of activity shows the enzyme has been denatured, so its chain has broken up into free amino acids
The changed amino acid supplies less energy to the reaction, so the substrate cannot react

questions.stem: Two short polypeptides, P and Q, are each made of the same five amino acids, but the amino acids are joined in a different order in P and in Q. Which statement about P and Q is correct?

options.text: They are the same molecule, because they contain exactly the same amino acids.
They have the same properties, because a polypeptide's properties come from its amine and carboxyl groups.
They are different polypeptides, because their R groups sit in different positions along the chain.
They are different polypeptides, because their peptide bonds join different pairs of R groups.

questions.explanation: Each chain has four peptide bonds and the same backbone, but the R groups are in a different order. Order is one of the three sources of variety, with chain length and repeats.
